nameStory: The American elm gets its name from being native to America, distinguishing it from European elms that early colonists knew from home. It's sometimes called 'white elm' because of its light-colored wood, or 'water elm' since it often grows near streams and wet areas.
description: The American elm is a majestic deciduous tree that can grow 60-80 feet tall with a graceful, vase-shaped crown. Its branches arch outward and upward like a fountain, creating the classic elm silhouette that once lined countless American streets. The tree has a straight trunk that divides into large spreading branches, and its leaves turn bright yellow in fall before dropping.

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Classic vase or wine glass shape with a straight trunk dividing into major branches that arch outward and upward, creating an umbrella-like canopy

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Oval leaves 3-6 inches long with doubly-serrated (double-toothed) edges and uneven bases where one side of the leaf extends further down the stem than the other

idTips.label: Bark
idTips.description: Gray-brown bark with deep, intersecting furrows creating diamond-shaped ridges on mature trees; feels rough and deeply grooved to the touch

idTips.label: Fruit/Seeds
idTips.description: Small, flat, oval-shaped winged seeds (samaras) about half an inch across that hang in clusters and flutter down like green confetti in late spring

idTips.label: Buds
idTips.description: Reddish-brown, pointed buds arranged alternately along twigs, with bud scales that overlap like shingles

habitat: American elms prefer moist, rich soils and are often found along streams, riverbanks, and floodplains throughout New England. They also grow in mixed hardwood forests, old fields, and were historically planted extensively as street trees in urban areas. Today, surviving specimens are scattered in parks, cemeteries, and rural areas where they escaped Dutch elm disease.

seasonality.spring: Small clusters of tiny reddish flowers appear before the leaves emerge, followed by the distinctive winged seeds that carpet the ground. New leaves unfurl bright green and soft to the touch.
seasonality.summer: Full canopy of dark green leaves creates dense shade, and the classic vase shape is most apparent when viewed from a distance.
seasonality.fall: Leaves turn bright yellow before dropping, revealing the elegant branching pattern. Seeds may be found scattered on the ground from spring's drop.
seasonality.winter: Bare branches show the distinctive vase-shaped architecture, and rough, furrowed bark is most visible. Pointed reddish buds help confirm identification.

funFact: American elms were once so beloved as street trees that entire cities were nicknamed 'Elm City' (like New Haven, Connecticut), but Dutch elm disease killed an estimated 75% of all American elms in North America - over 77 million trees - making it one of the most devastating ecological disasters in American history.
confusionNotes: The vase-shaped growth habit is the best way to distinguish American elm from other elms, which tend to have more rounded or irregular crowns. The uneven leaf bases (where one side extends further down the stem) are also diagnostic - run your finger along where the leaf meets the stem to feel this asymmetry.
contextualKnowledge: Dutch elm disease isn't actually from the Netherlands - it's named after the Dutch scientists who first studied it. The disease is caused by a fungus spread by bark beetles and devastated American elm populations starting in the 1920s, which is why these once-common street trees are now relatively rare.
compareHints: American elm's vase shape sets it apart from slippery elm, which has a more rounded crown and leaves that feel sandpapery on top. Siberian and Chinese elms (often called 'trash trees') have much smaller leaves and don't develop the classic American elm silhouette. If you see a large elm with the perfect vase shape, it's almost certainly an American elm.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Slippery elm differs from American elm by its smaller size, sandpaper-rough leaves, and reddish-brown hairy buds versus American elm's smooth leaves and smaller buds.
Siberian elm differs from native American elm by its much smaller leaves and more irregular growth habit, lacking the classic vase shape of American elm.
Unlike American elm with its classic vase shape and large leaves, Chinese elm has much smaller leaves and the distinctive exfoliating bark.
Compared to our native American elm, wych elm has much rougher, more textured leaves and different seed structure.
Compared to American elm, field elm is generally smaller with a broader crown and less pronounced vase shape.
Japanese elm is much smaller and more delicate than the mighty American elm, lacking that species' classic vase shape and towering height.
Unlike the American elm which has rougher leaf texture and more rigid movement, the fluttering elm's leaves have that distinctive dancing motion.
